  A body-mass index divides weight by a power of height. This note estimates
  that power for the women and men of a selected sport, or of the whole Rio
  2016 roster, from the log–log regression
  $\log w = \alpha + \beta \log h + \varepsilon,$ and compares it with the
  exponent of Quetelet's index, $\beta = 2$, and with the exponent of
  geometric similarity, $\beta = 3$.

# Introduction

Quetelet observed that adult weight grows roughly with the square of height
[@quetelet1842], and his ratio $w/h^2$ became the body-mass index
[@keys1972]. Benn proposed letting the population choose the power instead,
with the index $w/h^p$ [@benn1971]. Huxley's law of relative growth gives the
general form $w = a\,h^{\beta}$ [@huxley1932]. A body that keeps its shape as
it grows gains mass with its volume, so geometric similarity predicts
$\beta = 3$.

Choose a sport to refit every quantity in this note.

# Model

Taking logarithms turns the power law into a line. With $x_i = \log h_i$ and
$y_i = \log w_i$ for athlete $i$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i, \\
\E[\varepsilon_i \mid x_i] = 0,
\quad
\Var(\varepsilon_i \mid x_i) = \sigma^2,
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-model}

so that $w_i = e^{\alpha} h_i^{\beta} e^{\varepsilon_i}$. The exponent
$\beta$ is an elasticity: one percent more height goes with about $\beta$
percent more weight.

::: {#def-height-free}
## Height-free index

For a power $p$, the index $I_p = w / h^p$ is *height-free* when
$\Cov(\log I_p, \log h) = 0$.
:::

::: {#prp-exponent}
## The height-free power

The index $I_p$ is height-free exactly when

$$
p = \beta^\star = \frac{\Cov(\log w, \log h)}{\Var(\log h)},
$$ {#eq-beta-star}

the population slope in @eq-model.
:::

::: {.proof}
Since $\log I_p = \log w - p \log h$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Cov(\log I_p, \log h) \\
& \quad = \Cov(\log w, \log h) - p \Var(\log h),
\end{aligned}
$$
which vanishes if and only if $p = \Cov(\log w, \log h) / \Var(\log h)$.
:::

# Estimation

Stack the observations as $\vy = (y_1, \dots, y_n)^\T$ and

$$
X =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 \\
\vdots & \vdots \\
1 & x_n
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\vtheta =
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha \\
\beta
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Ordinary least squares minimizes $\lVert \vy - X \vtheta \rVert^2$. With
$S_{xx} = \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2$,
$S_{xy} = \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)$, and
$S_{yy} = \sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2$, the normal equations and their solution
are

$$
\begin{gathered}
X^\T X \hat\vtheta = X^\T \vy, \\
\hat\beta = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},
\qquad
\hat\alpha = \bar y - \hat\beta \bar x.
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-ols}

::: {#thm-gauss-markov}
## Gauss–Markov

Under @eq-model with uncorrelated errors, $\hat\vtheta$ has the smallest
variance among linear unbiased estimators of $\vtheta$.
:::

The residual variance and the standard error of the slope are

$$
\begin{gathered}
\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{S_{yy} - \hat\beta S_{xy}}{n - 2}, \\
\se(\hat\beta) = \frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \\
R^2 = 1 - \frac{S_{yy} - \hat\beta S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}.
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-se}

A test of $H_0\colon \beta = \beta_0$ and the 95% interval for $\beta$ use

$$
\begin{gathered}
t = \frac{\hat\beta - \beta_0}{\se(\hat\beta)} \sim t_{n-2}
\ \text{under } H_0, \\
\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975,\,n-2} \se(\hat\beta).
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-test}

The quantile $t_{0.975,\,n-2}$ follows from @eq-quantile in the appendix.

For the selected sport, the fitted power laws are

{{< marimo cell="scaling_relation" >}}

An exponent between 2 and 3 places the selection between the two reference
shapes: taller athletes are heavier than Quetelet's index allows for, and
lighter than a scaled copy of a shorter athlete. When the 95% interval lies
above 2, the body-mass index still rises with height in the selection, so it
reads tall athletes as heavier for their build. By @prp-exponent, the
height-free index for the selection divides weight by $h^{\hat\beta}$.

# Limitations

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## A cross-sectional roster

The roster of the Rio 2016 Olympic Games [@rio2016] is one cross-section of
elite athletes, selected by sport and qualification. The fit describes these athletes, not the general population.
Athletes from one national team share training and selection, so their errors
may correlate, and the standard errors in @tbl-fits are then too small. The
roster records sex in two categories, and athletes without a recorded height
or weight are excluded.
:::

# The quantile of Student's $t$ {.appendix .unnumbered}

With $\nu = n - 2$ degrees of freedom and the normal quantile
$z = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.95996$, the Cornish–Fisher expansion of Student's
$t$ gives [@abramowitz1964]

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{0.975,\,\nu}
\approx {} & z + \frac{z^3 + z}{4\nu} + \frac{5z^5 + 16z^3 + 3z}{96\nu^2} \\
& + \frac{3z^7 + 19z^5 + 17z^3 - 15z}{384\nu^3},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-quantile}

which is accurate to $10^{-4}$ from eight degrees of freedom. A group is
fitted only when it has at least ten athletes.
